title: You Are Not Alone With Postpartum Depression
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (the transcript labels him iHeart Intro in places) discuss postpartum depression as a "Bummer Edition" public-service episode. They cover maternal mental health umbrella terms, including postpartum anxiety, perinatal OCD, postnatal mood and anxiety disorder, and postpartum psychosis, along with symptoms, risk factors, and racial disparities in screening and treatment. They also explain the hormonal drop after birth (progesterone, estrogen, oxytocin, and allopregnanolone), the role of sleep loss, treatment options (CBT, medication, SSRIs considered safe in breastfeeding such as sertraline and paroxetine, and the brexanolone and zuranolone drugs with their cost), postpartum depression in fathers, and the cost of childcare. The episode ends with listener mail about professional wrestler Adam Bomb and the Three Mile Island episode.
topics: racial disparities in maternal mental health

entities.name: Jackson Hogue Phillips Contextualized Stress Measure

segments.title: Bummer Edition introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the sad, joke-free Bummer Edition episode as a public service on postpartum depression, noting prevalence estimates of about one in eight women and the stigma that keeps many from seeking help.

segments.title: Stigma, pressure, and maternal mental health umbrella
segments.summary: The hosts discuss stigma against new mothers, the pressure to be a perfect mom immediately, and the umbrella term maternal mental health, stressing the need to ask for help and to offer it.

segments.title: Terminology and US maternal mortality statistics
segments.summary: The hosts explain that postpartum depression can start during pregnancy or up to a year after birth. They cite CDC figures on rising rates and say suicide and drug overdose are the leading causes of postpartum maternal death in the US.

segments.title: Undiagnosis, baby blues, and symptoms
segments.summary: The hosts explain that about half of cases go undiagnosed and that baby blues differ from PPD mainly in severity and duration. They list symptoms and note that PPD can start weeks or months after birth.

segments.title: Postpartum psychosis and risk factors
segments.summary: The hosts describe postpartum psychosis as a medical emergency involving delusions, paranoia, and disorientation, which is rare at about one in a thousand births. They discuss bipolar history and sleep loss as risk factors.

segments.title: Further risk factors for PPD
segments.summary: The hosts list risk factors including prior depression or anxiety, childhood trauma, infertility treatment, unplanned pregnancy, low income, anemia, hypothyroidism, and a possible genetic component.

segments.title: Perinatal OCD and intrusive thoughts
segments.summary: The hosts describe postpartum OCD, which comes on quickly after birth and involves checking, contamination fears, and intrusive thoughts. They stress that such thoughts do not define the mother and that support helps.

segments.title: Postnatal mood and anxiety disorder and a support podcast
segments.summary: The hosts describe a feedback loop in which bonding anxiety affects the baby and worsens the mother's anxiety. Chuck recommends the podcast One Bad Mother as a source of support.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break taken before the statistics section on racial disparities.

segments.title: Racial disparities in PPD prevalence and treatment
segments.summary: The hosts cite higher PPD rates among Black and Latina mothers and lower treatment rates. They explain that symptoms may present differently and that the Jackson Hogue Phillips Contextualized Stress Measure was developed for Black mothers. They note that under 20 percent of women are screened.
topics: Jackson Hogue Phillips Contextualized Stress Measure

segments.title: Social determinants and causes of PPD
segments.summary: The hosts argue that the underlying causes are the same across groups and that disparities come from social determinants of health such as income, environment, and access to care. They describe the hormonal and life-change stress that come with a newborn.

segments.title: Hormones after birth
segments.summary: The hosts describe how pregnancy hormones such as progesterone, estrogen, relaxin, and oxytocin rise and then fall back within about 72 hours after birth, and how this swing contributes to PPD.

segments.title: Environmental factors and the role of sleep and support
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how new-baby life, including sleep deprivation, physical recovery, and isolation, combines with hormones to cause the baby blues and PPD. They urge partners to share night feedings and recommend getting out into the world.

segments.title: Allopregnanolone and effects on the baby
segments.summary: The hosts identify allopregnanolone, a neurosteroid that drops sharply after birth, as a main hormonal culprit. They say PPD is linked to preterm birth and low birth weight, which also affects bonding.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break before the treatment section.

segments.title: Treatment options and medication costs
segments.summary: The hosts cover therapy, CBT, antidepressants, and the allopregnanolone-targeted drugs brexanolone and zuranolone. They discuss the high out-of-pocket cost of those drugs and say SSRIs such as sertraline and paroxetine are considered compatible with breastfeeding.

segments.title: Sponsor read for Zuranolone
segments.summary: Sponsor read for a PPD drug, with a short joke exchange.

segments.title: Postpartum depression in fathers and childcare costs
segments.summary: The hosts say about 8 to 10 percent of new fathers experience depression or anxiety, usually three to six months after birth. They discuss the added pressure on dads and US childcare costs, and Chuck urges voters to support free childcare.

segments.title: Testosterone, closing remarks, and feedback
segments.summary: The hosts note that testosterone drops in fathers during pregnancy and after birth. They reflect on how the episode went and invite listener feedback.

segments.title: Listener mail: Adam Bomb and Three Mile Island
segments.summary: A listener from Michigan named Adam says the Three Mile Island episode omitted wrestler Adam Bomb. The hosts thank him and mention a DJ named Adam Bomb.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener email and close the episode.
